title: The Binomial Series
short: (1 + x)ᵏ as a series for any k.

blocks.html: The binomial theorem expands $(1 + x)^{k}$ when $k$ is a whole number, and the expansion stops. Newton noticed that the same pattern works for any exponent, like $k = \frac{1}{2}$ or $k = -1$, except that the series never stops. It is a known series you can build from Taylor coefficients.

For $f(x) = (1 + x)^{k}$: $f'(x) = k(1 + x)^{k-1}$, $f''(x) = k(k - 1)(1 + x)^{k-2}$, and in general $f^{(n)}(0) = k(k - 1)\cdots(k - n + 1)$. Dividing by $n!$ gives the coefficient
$$\binom{k}{n} = \frac{k(k - 1)\cdots(k - n + 1)}{n!}.$$
When $k$ is a whole number, a factor $(k - k)$ eventually appears and every later coefficient is 0: the familiar finite expansion. Otherwise the series goes on forever, and the ratio test gives radius 1.

blocks.q: Find the first four terms of the series for $\sqrt{1 + x}$.

blocks.name: taylor
blocks.cap: Partial sums of the binomial series for $\sqrt{1 + x}$. Inside $|x| < 1$ they close in on the curve; past $x = 1$ they eventually wander off.

blocks.title: Substituting
blocks.q: Find the first three nonzero terms for $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}$.
steps: Integrating this term by term gives the series for $\arcsin x$.

blocks.html: Using the series on $(a + x)^{k}$ without factoring out $a$. The formula needs the form $(1 + u)^{k}$. For $\sqrt{4 + x}$, write $2\left(1 + \frac{x}{4}\right)^{1/2} = 2 + \frac{x}{4} - \frac{x^{2}}{64} + \cdots$, which converges for $|x| < 4$, not $|x| < 1$. Check: at $x = 0$ the series must give $f(0) = 2$.
